concept.name: Autocorrelation function
concept.definition: The full set of autocorrelations of a time series viewed as a function of the lag h, usually plotted as a correlogram with confidence bands. The ACF's shape (exponential decay, cutoff, oscillation) characterizes the dependence structure and guides model identification.
concept.intuition: Instead of asking whether the series depends on its past at one specific lag, the ACF scans all lags at once, revealing the memory profile of the series.
concept.mechanics: The theoretical ACF of a stationary process is rho(h) = gamma(h)/gamma(0); the sample ACF plots R_h = C_h/C_0 against h = 1, 2, ... with approximate 95% bands of +/-1.96/sqrt(N) under the null of white noise. MA(q) processes show an ACF that cuts off after lag q; AR processes show decaying ACFs.
concept.formula: rho(h) = Cov(X_t, X_{t+h}) / Var(X_t); sample estimate R_h = C_h / C_0 with C_h = (1/N)*sum_{t=1}^{N-h}(Y_t - Ybar)(Y_{t+h} - Ybar).
concept.failure_modes: For non-stationary series the sample ACF decays very slowly, mimicking strong persistence and misleading identification. With many lags examined, some spuriously exceed the confidence bands by chance (roughly 5% under the null).
concept.misconceptions: That any ACF spike outside the bands proves exploitable predictability; at 20 lags about one spike is expected by chance, and statistical significance is not economic significance after costs.
concept.example: The ACF of squared daily stock returns decays slowly over many lags, revealing long memory in volatility even though raw returns show almost no autocorrelation.

citations.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, Section 1.3.3.1 Autocorrelation Plot
